stages.title: Atmospheric properties
stages.hook: Climb a very tall mountain and breathing gets harder, and it gets colder. What is changing in the air as you go up?
explain: The atmosphere is the blanket of gas around Earth. It is mostly nitrogen (about 78%) and oxygen (about 21%). Air has mass, pressure, temperature and density. Density is how much mass is packed into each cubic metre.

At sea level, in standard conditions, air has a density of about 1.225 kg/m³, a pressure of about 101 325 pascals (Pa) and a temperature of 15 °C. Higher up there is less air above, so pressure and density both fall. That is why the air is 'thin' on high mountains.

In the lowest layer, the troposphere, the temperature falls by about 6.5 °C for every kilometre you climb, up to roughly 11 km. Most airliners cruise near the top of this layer. Wings and engines make less force in thin air, so altitude changes how an aircraft performs.

example.q: A room measures 5 m × 4 m × 3 m. Use 1.225 kg/m³ for air. What is the mass of the air in the room?

analogies.sea: Dive deeper in the sea and the water above presses harder. In air, being low down means more air above you, so pressure is larger.
analogies.home: A stack of pillows: the bottom pillow is squashed most. The bottom of the atmosphere is squashed most too.
analogies.city: A crowded train carriage near the door is packed tight. Air near the ground is packed tighter than air high up.
analogies.nature: Mountain climbers breathe more slowly and tire quickly because each breath contains less oxygen.

stages.mnemonic: Up, up, up: less air, less push, more cold!
terms: Mass in each cubic metre, in kg/m³.
Force pushing on each square metre, in pascals (Pa).
The lowest layer of the atmosphere, where weather happens.

misc.wrong: Air has no weight, so it cannot push on anything.
misc.right: Air has mass. At sea level one cubic metre has about 1.2 kg, and the air pressing on us is about 101 kPa.

stages.limits: These are standard-atmosphere values. Real air changes with weather, place and season.

teach.topic: Why air is thinner high up

stages.title: Four forces of flight
stages.hook: A passenger jet cruises at a steady speed and height for hours. If forces are acting on it all the time, why is it not speeding up, rising or sinking?
explain: Four forces act on an aircraft. Weight pulls it down. Lift pushes it up. Thrust pushes it forward. Drag pulls it back. Forces are measured in newtons (N).

Weight equals mass times the gravitational field strength: W = m × g, where g = 9.81 N/kg (or 9.81 m/s²) near the ground. If lift equals weight, the aircraft does not climb or sink. If thrust equals drag, it keeps its speed. This is steady, level flight.
If forces are unbalanced, Newton's second law applies: resultant force = mass × acceleration. More thrust than drag makes the aircraft speed up. More lift than weight makes it climb.

example.q: A 1000 kg aircraft has thrust 5000 N and drag 3000 N. What is its acceleration? (Assume level flight.)

analogies.sea: A rowing boat at steady speed: the push from the oars equals the water's drag.
analogies.sport: A cyclist at steady speed pedals just hard enough to match the air resistance.
analogies.city: A lift moving at steady speed has the cable pull equal to its weight.
analogies.farm: A tractor pulling a plough at steady speed: the engine force matches the soil's resistance.

stages.mnemonic: Up is Lift, down is Weight, forward is Thrust, back is Drag. Balanced, it flies straight.

stages.title: Wing and airfoil geometry
stages.hook: Cut a wing slice along the flight direction and you do not find a flat board. Why do engineers shape it so carefully?
explain: The cross-section of a wing is called an airfoil. Its front edge is the leading edge and its back edge is the trailing edge. The straight line joining them is the chord. The curved line halfway between the top and bottom surfaces is the camber line.

Seen from above, the distance from wingtip to wingtip is the span. The wing area S is the planform area. For a rectangular wing, area = span × chord. Aspect ratio is span² ÷ area, which for a rectangular wing equals span ÷ chord.

The angle between the chord and the oncoming air is the angle of attack. Many gliders have long, thin wings with a high aspect ratio, which suits efficient flight. Short, stubby wings suit strong, fast manoeuvres.

example.q: A rectangular wing has span 12 m and chord 1.5 m. What are its area and aspect ratio?

analogies.sea: A sailing boat's sail has a leading edge facing the wind and a trailing edge behind, just like a wing.
analogies.nature: An albatross has long narrow wings (high aspect ratio) for gliding over oceans. A sparrow has short wide wings for quick turns.
analogies.sport: A surfboard's front is its nose; its length is like the chord.
analogies.city: A cross-section of a bridge beam shows its shape in the same way an airfoil shows a wing.

stages.mnemonic: Leading edge leads, trailing edge trails, chord is the line between, span is the width.
terms: The straight line from leading edge to trailing edge.
The distance from wingtip to wingtip.
Span squared divided by wing area.
The angle between the chord and the oncoming air.

misc.wrong: The angle of attack is the same as the angle the aircraft's nose points above the horizon.
misc.right: Angle of attack is measured between the chord and the airflow. In a climb the nose can point up while the angle of attack is small, or in a descent it can be large.

stages.limits: Real wings are often tapered, swept and twisted, so the simple span × chord formula is only exact for rectangular wings.

stages.title: Lift generation
stages.hook: Some people say the air over the top of a wing must 'catch up' with the air below. Is that how lift really works?
explain: A wing makes lift by changing the airflow. It turns the air downward, and by Newton's third law the air pushes the wing up. At the same time the air over the top moves faster and its pressure drops, while the pressure under the wing is higher. This pressure difference over the wing's area is the lift force. These are two views of the same event.

The equal transit time idea (the air on top must travel further so it must rush to meet the air below) is a misconception. The air above actually arrives at the trailing edge before the air from below. Speed is not set by a need to meet up.

Engineers use the lift equation: L = ½ × ρ × v² × S × C_L. Here ρ is air density, v is speed, S is wing area and C_L is the lift coefficient, which depends on airfoil shape and angle of attack. Lift grows with the square of speed, so doubling the speed makes four times the lift.

example.q: A wing has area 10 m² and C_L = 1.0. It flies at 40 m/s at sea level (ρ = 1.225 kg/m³). Find the lift.
steps: Write L = ½ × ρ × v² × S × C_L.

analogies.sea: A paddle pushes water backward and the canoe goes forward. A wing pushes air downward and is pushed up.
analogies.sport: Hold your hand flat out of a car window at a slight tilt (with an adult, safely). It rises as air is deflected downward.
analogies.home: A hair dryer's air hitting a tilted tray pushes the tray up and away.
analogies.nature: A bird tilts its wings to climb, which turns more air downward.

stages.mnemonic: Turn the air down, get pushed up. Pressure low on top, higher below.

A number showing how well a wing makes lift (C_L).
Higher pressure below, lower above, giving a net upward force.
A false idea that air above and below must reach the back together.

misc.wrong: Air over the top of a wing must meet up with the air below, so it travels faster to catch up.
misc.right: This 'equal transit time' idea is a myth. Air over the top actually gets to the trailing edge first. Lift comes from the wing turning the flow downward and from lower pressure on top, which are linked.

stages.limits: The lift equation is a model that packs the details into C_L. Real lift depends on flow conditions, and at high speed or large angles it behaves differently.

stages.title: Aircraft stability fundamentals
stages.hook: A paper dart with the wrong weight in the nose tumbles; one with the right balance glides steadily. Why does balance matter?
explain: An aircraft is stable if, after a small disturbance such as a gust, it tends to return to its original flight. It is unstable if the disturbance grows, and neutrally stable if it just stays disturbed.

Balance depends on the centre of gravity (CG), where the weight acts, and the centre of pressure, where the lift effectively acts. The tailplane, a small wing at the back, helps by pushing down or up to keep the nose steady. A CG that is too far back makes an aircraft hard or impossible to control.

Aircraft move about three axes: pitch (nose up and down), roll (one wing up, the other down) and yaw (nose left or right). Each axis can be stable. A tail fin helps yaw stability, and wings angled slightly upward (dihedral) help roll stability.

example.q: A seesaw has a 20 kg child 2 m from the pivot. How heavy is a child on the other side if 1 m from the pivot, to balance it?
steps: Balance when mass × distance matches on both sides.

analogies.sea: A boat with a heavy keel rights itself after a wave. That is stability.
analogies.sport: A bicycle is stable when rolling but wobbles at very slow speeds.
analogies.home: A ball in a bowl rolls back to the middle (stable). A ball on top of an upside-down bowl rolls away (unstable).
analogies.farm: A loaded cart with the load far back may tip its front up.

stages.mnemonic: Ball in a bowl comes back; ball on a hill rolls away.

The point where the weight seems to act.
Tilting one wing up and the other down.

misc.wrong: More stable is always better for every aircraft.
misc.right: Very stable aircraft are harder to manoeuvre. Airliners favour stability; some fighters are made nearly unstable so they respond fast, with computers helping to control them.

stages.limits: This level uses simple ideas. Full stability analysis uses equations for forces and moments about each axis.

stages.title: Aircraft control surfaces
stages.hook: A plane has no steering wheel. How does the pilot make it climb, dip or turn?
explain: Control surfaces are movable parts of the wings and tail. Moving one changes the airflow around it and so changes the force on the aircraft. The pilot uses them to turn the aircraft about its three axes.

Elevators on the tailplane control pitch: raising the elevator pushes the tail down and the nose up. Ailerons on the wing tips control roll: one goes up while the other goes down. The rudder on the tail fin controls yaw.

To turn, a pilot banks (rolls) the aircraft using the ailerons, so the lift tilts toward the inside of the turn. The rudder keeps the turn coordinated. Flaps on the inner wings change the wing's shape to make more lift at low speeds, which helps with take-off and landing.

example.q: The pilot wants the nose to rise. Which surface moves, and how?
steps: Nose up and down is pitch.
Raise the elevator trailing edge so the tail is pushed down and the nose lifts.

analogies.sea: A boat's rudder swings to turn the boat. The plane's rudder turns its nose left or right.
analogies.sport: A diver tucks or stretches arms to turn in the air, like moving control surfaces.
analogies.home: A door hinge: a small movable flap changes a bigger thing's behaviour.
analogies.city: A bus driver turns a wheel to steer; a pilot moves control surfaces.

stages.mnemonic: Elevator = nose up/down, Ailerons = roll, Rudder = yaw.
terms: Surface that adds lift at low speed.

misc.wrong: A plane turns by using the rudder alone, like a boat.
misc.right: A plane mainly turns by banking: the tilted lift force pulls it round. The rudder only helps keep the turn smooth.

stages.limits: Many aircraft also use spoilers, trim tabs and fly-by-wire computers. Controls and names vary between designs.

questions.q: Explain how raising the elevator makes the aircraft's nose go up.
questions.model: Raising the elevator changes the tailplane's shape so the tail gets a downward force. The tail goes down and the nose rises.
questions.why: The elevator changes the tail's lift, which rotates the aircraft about its pitch axis.

questions.q: Why are ailerons on the wing tips, not near the fuselage?

Wing tips are warmer, so the controls work better
Air is thicker at the tips than near the body

panel.q: A car turns with its wheels. Why can't a plane turn the same way on its own in the air?

panel.why: Total lift must rise in a turn so its vertical part still equals weight.

stages.title: Aircraft propulsion
stages.hook: A propeller plane and a jet airliner look very different, but both push air backward. Why does pushing air back move a plane forward?
explain: Thrust is made by pushing a lot of air (or gas) backward. By Newton's third law, the air pushes the aircraft forward. A propeller is a set of spinning twisted blades, which act like small rotating wings that pull the aircraft forward. It accelerates a large amount of air by a small amount.

A jet engine takes in air, compresses it, burns fuel with it and shoots hot gas out of the back much faster than the incoming air. A turbofan, used on airliners, also has a big fan that pushes extra air around the core, which is efficient and quieter.

A useful number is thrust-to-weight ratio: thrust divided by weight. A ratio above 1 means the engines could lift the aircraft straight up; most airliners are about 0.2 to 0.3, while rockets and some fighters are above 1.

example.q: A model rocket has mass 0.5 kg and its motor gives 15 N of thrust. Use g = 9.81 m/s². What is the thrust-to-weight ratio?

analogies.sea: A motorboat's propeller pushes water back and the boat moves forward.
analogies.home: A desk fan blows air one way and, on wheels, would be pushed the other way.
analogies.sport: A swimmer pushes water behind them to move ahead.
analogies.nature: A squid squirts water backward to shoot forward.

stages.mnemonic: Push air back, plane goes ahead. Thrust over weight tells you if it can climb straight up.
terms: Twisted spinning blades that push air backward.
An engine that makes thrust from a fast jet of hot gas.
A jet engine with a large fan that moves extra air.

misc.wrong: A jet pushes against the air behind it, so it could not work in space.
misc.right: Thrust comes from throwing mass backward, not from pushing on outside air. Rockets carry their own propellant and work in space; jet engines need air for burning, so they do not.

stages.limits: Engine performance depends on speed, altitude and air density. The simple thrust-to-weight number is for one moment, not the whole flight.

stages.title: Basic flight manoeuvres
stages.hook: Every flight has the same basic steps: take off, climb, cruise, descend and land. What does the pilot change at each step?
explain: Take-off: the aircraft speeds up on the runway until its wings make more lift than its weight. Then the pilot raises the nose a little (rotation) and it leaves the ground.

Climb: the aircraft needs extra lift or power to gain height. Cruise is steady level flight. In a descent the pilot lowers power or the nose, and the aircraft trades height for speed or lower power. A glider turns height into forward motion.

In a turn the aircraft banks, so part of the lift points sideways and pulls the flight path round. Landing reverses take-off: the pilot slows down, extends flaps, lines up with the runway, and flares gently so the wheels touch the runway softly.

stages.title: Rocket motion fundamentals
stages.hook: Rockets work in empty space where there is nothing to push against. And to stay in orbit, a satellite must be going very fast sideways. Why?
explain: A rocket makes thrust by throwing propellant out of its nozzle at high speed. By Newton's third law, the propellant pushes the rocket the other way. To lift off, thrust must be bigger than weight, so the thrust-to-weight ratio must be above 1.

As fuel burns, the rocket gets lighter, so the same thrust gives more acceleration. A rocket also drops empty tanks in stages so it does not carry dead weight. The more speed needed and the lower the exhaust speed, the more propellant is required. That idea is the rocket equation, which you will meet later with numbers.

A satellite stays up because it is falling around Earth. It moves sideways so fast, about 7.8 km/s (7800 m/s) for a low orbit, that as it falls the ground curves away beneath it. It is not 'beyond gravity': gravity there is still strong.

example.q: A rocket of mass 500 kg has thrust 10 000 N. Use g = 9.81 m/s², ignoring air resistance. What is its upward acceleration at lift-off?

analogies.nature: A squid ejects water to jet away.
analogies.tech: A space probe uses small thrusters to adjust its path.

stages.mnemonic: Throw mass back, go forward. To orbit, go sideways fast and keep falling around.

A part of a rocket dropped once its fuel is used up.

misc.wrong: Astronauts float in orbit because there is no gravity there.
misc.right: Gravity at orbit height is about 90% of its value at the ground. Astronauts float because they and their spacecraft are in free fall together.

stages.limits: The numbers here ignore air drag and the Earth's rotation. Real launches follow carefully planned curved paths. The game is educational and does not replace real engineering training.

panel.q: Why does a rocket's acceleration increase during burn even if thrust stays constant?
panel.model: As propellant burns, the rocket's mass falls. With the same thrust, a = F ÷ m gets larger, so acceleration rises.
panel.why: Newton's second law with decreasing mass.

panel.why: Orbit needs large sideways speed, so the path gradually turns toward horizontal.
